title: Uncovering Latent Structures in Robust Pulse Sequences: A Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Approach for Adaptable Quantum Control
authors: Tobias Kiermeyer, Thomas Heydenreich, Léo Van Damme, Sebastian Hohenemser, Florian Marquardt, Steffen J. Glaser
abstract: Real-time adaptive control of quantum systems requires rapid generation of robust, high-fidelity pulses across a continuous range of operating conditions. Standard optimization algorithms such as gradient-ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) solve each instance independently, discarding information between runs and requiring costly reinitialization when parameters change. We present an approach to robust optimal quantum control based on model-based reinforcement learning, in which a single neural network -- embedding the Hamiltonian directly into the training pipeline -- generates robust gates across an entire family of gate configurations, without pre-computed training data. Demonstrated on a single-spin (two-level) system, the trained networks produce pulses for arbitrary rotation angles over a range of pulse durations, detunings, and field inhomogeneities in milliseconds, at fidelities comparable to multi-seed GRAPE. The framework is inherently adaptable: any parameter entering the Hamiltonian can serve as a network input, extending the approach to different systems and control settings. Beyond speed, the network reveals structure in the control landscape: it discovers the same structured phase profiles that appear in GRAPE solutions -- made identifiable through fidelity-invariant symmetry transformations -- but more consistently than independent optimization. This consistency enables smooth interpolation across the entire trained parameter space.
summary: The paper introduces a novel model-based Reinforcement Learning framework to solve the challenge of generating quantum control pulses that remain high-fidelity despite variations in experimental parameters. By training a single neural network on an entire family of gate configurations, it achieves rapid, adaptable pulse generation superior to traditional methods like GRAPE for exploring parameter space robustness. This significantly accelerates the design cycle for complex quantum operations.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving real-time, adaptive quantum control by generating robust, high-fidelity control pulses across a continuous range of varying experimental parameters.
main_result: A model-based Reinforcement Learning approach using a single neural network can generate highly accurate and adaptable control pulses that maintain fidelity comparable to multiple independent optimization runs (GRAPE).
method: The authors train a neural network to map input gate configurations directly to optimized pulse phase profiles, bypassing the need for iterative optimization for every parameter set.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a single-spin (two-level) quantum system driven by an external field, described by a time-dependent Hamiltonian that includes tunable parameters like detuning and inhomogeneity.
key_observables: Fidelity ($\mathcal{J}$) and ensemble-averaged infidelity ($ ar{\mathcal{J}}$), which quantify how well the generated pulse achieves the target gate operation across parameter variations.
important_parameters: Gate configuration parameters include rotation angle ($ eta$), pulse duration ($T_P$), detuning range width ($\Delta\delta$), and amplitude inhomogeneity range width ($\Delta s$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the underlying physical model (Hamiltonian) can be embedded into a differentiable computational graph for training. GRAPE's memoryless nature is contrasted with the network's ability to generalize.
figures_summary: Figures compare pulse phase profiles and robustness fingerprints ($\log_{10} J(\delta)$) generated by the NN versus standard GRAPE, demonstrating structural consistency across varying parameters and durations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of adaptive control limitations in traditional methods (GRAPE), proposes the model-based RL framework using a single network to learn the entire parameter manifold, details the training process involving ensemble averaging, and validates performance by comparing generalization capabilities against multi-seed GRAPE runs.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful machine learning tool for quantum control, moving beyond computationally expensive, point-wise optimization methods. The ability to encode system physics directly into the loss function makes it highly relevant for designing robust protocols in experimental AMO platforms like superconducting qubits or trapped ions.
